title: CIC 1 Task 3
listening_script: OK, so… this shows up in schools all the time. Let me give you two cases. First, a few years ago, our district tried to boost recreational reading with a pizza-coupon program. If students read a certain number of pages each week, they got a free slice. At first, the numbers looked great—lots of kids logged pages. But, uh, two things happened. One, students started choosing the shortest books they could find, just to hit the target. And two, when the coupons ended, their reading dropped below where it had been before. In other words, they began reading for the pizza, not for the pleasure of the stories, and when the reward disappeared, so did the motivation. Second, there’s a classic study with preschoolers and drawing. Some children were told ahead of time they’d get a fancy certificate for drawing—so the reward was expected. Another group drew and then, surprise, they received a certificate—unexpected. A third group got no reward. Later, when researchers simply offered markers during free play, the kids who had expected a reward spent less time drawing and seemed less interested. The other two groups drew just as much as before. So, in both cases—the pizza coupons and the drawing study—an expected, controlling reward shifted attention from “I do this because I like it” to “I do this to get something.”
question_text: Using points from the lecture, explain the overjustification effect and how the professor’s examples illustrate this concept.
reading_body: The overjustification effect occurs when offering external rewards for an activity that people already find enjoyable reduces their intrinsic motivation to do that activity. When a reward is introduced, individuals may begin to attribute their behavior to the reward rather than to their own interest. As a result, once the reward is removed, participation and enjoyment often decline. This shift is most likely when the reward is expected in advance and feels controlling (for example, “Do this to get that”). In contrast, rewards that are unexpected or framed as informational recognition of good performance are less likely to undermine intrinsic interest.

title: CIC 2 Task 3
listening_script: OK, so… let me give you an example from agriculture, since that’s where this principle was first observed. Uh, imagine a farmer who owns a fixed amount of land… let’s say ten acres. At first, when he hires more workers to plant and harvest crops, productivity goes up a lot, because there’s more labor to get the work done. But after a certain number of workers, things start to get crowded. Workers have to wait for others to finish a task before they can start their own, so each new worker adds less and less to the total harvest. And if the farmer keeps hiring beyond that point, people might actually get in each other’s way, and total output could even drop. Another example is studying for an exam. Suppose you study for two hours — your understanding of the material might improve a lot. If you study for four hours, you’ll still improve, but maybe not as much as before. And if you push it to ten hours straight without a break, you might be so tired and unfocused that you actually start forgetting things. So in both cases, after a certain point, adding more input — whether it’s workers or study time — results in smaller gains, and sometimes even lower output. That’s the Law of Diminishing Returns.
question_text: Using the examples from the lecture, explain the law of diminishing returns and its effects.
reading_body: In economics, the law of diminishing returns describes a situation in which adding more of one input to a fixed quantity of other inputs eventually results in smaller and smaller increases in output. At first, additional resources may significantly boost productivity, but after a certain point, each new unit of input contributes less to the overall result. In some cases, output may even decrease. This principle applies to many areas, including agriculture, manufacturing, and studying. It emphasizes the importance of balancing resources efficiently, rather than assuming that more input will always lead to proportionally greater productivity.

title: CIC 3 Task 3
listening_script: OK, so… let me give you two cases that really show this. First, there’s a classic problem-solving task with a candle, a box of tacks, and some matches. Participants are asked to attach the candle to a wall so it can burn without dripping wax on the table. Now, when the tacks are presented inside the box, people usually see the box only as a container and they struggle; they try tacking the candle itself to the wall, which doesn’t work. But if the tacks are placed next to an empty box, more people suddenly realize they can pin the box to the wall and set the candle on the box. Same materials—different presentation—but noticing the box as a platform instead of a container reduces functional fixedness. Second, uh, a quick example from my classroom. Our projector remote wouldn’t stay closed because the battery cover had snapped off. Students kept saying, “We need tape,” because, you know, that’s the normal fix. No tape. So I asked, “What properties do we need?” We need pressure to hold the batteries in place. One student pulled a rubber band off a notebook, wrapped it around the remote, and—done. By focusing on the function (apply pressure) rather than the usual object (tape), she bypassed functional fixedness and solved the problem in seconds. So in both cases—reframing the box and repurposing a rubber band—shifting attention from an object’s typical use to its features leads to a creative, effective solution, exactly as the reading describes.
question_text: Using the examples from the lecture, explain the concept of functional fixedness.
reading_body: Functional fixedness is a cognitive tendency that limits people to seeing objects only in terms of their usual, intended uses. This bias can interfere with problem solving because individuals overlook alternative properties of an object—its weight, shape, or material—that might make it useful in a new way. Functional fixedness is strongest when an object’s typical function is highly familiar or has just been emphasized. However, it can be reduced when people are encouraged to describe objects by their features rather than by their conventional purpose, or when the context highlights a novel use. Overcoming functional fixedness often leads to more flexible, creative solutions.

title: CIC 4 Task 3
listening_script: Here are two cases that make this idea really clear. First, consider desert plants. In the Americas you’ve got cacti, and in Africa there are unrelated plants in the spurge family that look strikingly similar—thick, water-storing stems and sharp spines. To a casual observer, they seem like the same kind of plant. But internally, they’re built differently. In many cacti, the spines are modified leaves and the green, fleshy stem does most of the photosynthesis. In many spurges, the protective structures develop from different tissues, and the arrangement of the vascular system isn’t the same. Same problem—hot, dry climate—so both lineages evolved a compact, spiny, water-saving body plan independently. Second, think about small gliding mammals. In North America and Eurasia you have flying squirrels; in Australia there are sugar gliders. They’re not close relatives, but both groups have a stretchy membrane between the forelimbs and hind limbs that lets them glide from tree to tree. The lifestyle—moving efficiently through forest canopies, escaping predators, reaching scattered food—pushes both lineages toward the same aerodynamic solution. If you look closer, though, the details of bone proportions, dentition, and developmental timing differ, which tells us the gliding membrane evolved separately. So, in both cases—desert succulents and gliding mammals—the organisms face similar ecological pressures and end up with similar functional traits, but those traits come from different origins. That pattern is exactly what we mean by convergent evolution, as the reading explains.
question_text: Using points from the lecture, explain convergent evolution and how the professor’s examples illustrate this concept.
reading_body: Convergent evolution occurs when unrelated organisms independently evolve similar traits because they face similar environmental pressures or occupy similar ecological niches. The resulting features are analogous: they perform the same function or look alike, but they do not arise from a recent common ancestor. Convergence is common in organisms that live in comparable habitats—deserts, oceans, or forest canopies—where similar challenges repeatedly favor similar solutions. Distinguishing convergence from homology (similarity due to shared ancestry) often requires examining internal structure and developmental origin. If two traits serve the same purpose but are built from different underlying parts or tissues, they are likely products of convergent evolution rather than inheritance.

title: CIC 5 Task 3
listening_script: Right, so, here are two examples that make this really concrete. First of all, think about a tiny hummingbird. It burns energy fast, and at night the temperature drops while there’s no food coming in. So many hummingbirds enter daily torpor. Their body temperature falls, heart rate slows way down, and they sit very still on a branch through the night. Then, when the sun comes up, they warm themselves—sometimes you can see a little shiver—and within a short time they’re back to normal, flying and feeding. That’s classic short-term torpor: just long enough to get through the night when energy is tight. Then, consider a ground squirrel that faces a long, cold winter with little food. Instead of nightly torpor, it goes into hibernation. It curls up in an underground burrow, its temperature drops close to the surroundings, and its metabolism becomes extremely low for weeks at a time. Every so often, it briefly wakes, warms up, and then goes back down again, but overall it spends most of the season in that low-energy state. Hibernation carries the same idea as torpor—save energy—but stretched across an entire season when conditions are poor. So, in both cases—hummingbirds at night and ground squirrels in winter—the animal lowers temperature and metabolism to conserve energy, with the main difference being duration: hours for torpor, weeks or months for hibernation.
question_text: Using points and examples from the lecture, explain torpor and hibernation and their diffrences.
reading_body: Torpor is a temporary state in which an animal lowers its body temperature and slows its metabolism to conserve energy. It usually lasts hours or a day and is used when food is scarce or temperatures are extreme. Hibernation is a longer, seasonal form of torpor that can continue for weeks or months. In both cases, the animal reduces energy use and becomes less active, then later warms up and returns to normal. Whether an animal uses short daily torpor or long hibernation depends on its size, environment, and food supply. These strategies help small birds and mammals survive periods when keeping a normal body temperature would be too costly.

title: CIC 6 Task 3
listening_script: Let's take a look at two everyday cases of this phenomenon. We can take the example of a bilingual student—let’s call her María. In a literature seminar she answers the professor in standard academic English: careful pronunciation, complete sentences, formal vocabulary. After class, she’s walking with friends who also speak Spanish, and the conversation slides naturally into Spanglish—mostly English, but with Spanish words for family or food, little expressions that feel warmer. Later, at home, María visits her grandmother who prefers Spanish, so she switches fully to Spanish and also uses respectful forms of address. Notice what’s happening: same person, three settings, and she adjusts not because she can’t speak one language, but to match audience, show respect, and include others. We can also consider style-shifting within one language. Another student—let’s call him Chad—works the evening desk at the residence hall. When a parent calls with a concern, Chad uses a more formal register—"Good evening. How may I assist you?"—clear diction, no slang. Two minutes later, a classmate stops by to ask about a package, and Chad switches to a casual style—"Hey, what's up? Yeah, it came in this morning; you just need your ID." Same speaker, same language, but a shift in vocabulary and tone to fit the relationship and the goals of the interaction.
question_text: Using points and examples from the lecture, explain code-switching.
reading_body: Code-switching is the practice of shifting between languages, dialects, or levels of formality depending on the situation and audience. Rather than indicating poor language ability, code-switching is usually a strategic choice that helps speakers manage social relationships, show respect or solidarity, and make messages clearer. People may switch to match a listener’s preferences, to fit a setting (like a classroom versus a family dinner), or to signal identity. Code-switching also includes style-shifting within one language—moving from informal to formal speech. Researchers study when switches occur and what social meanings they carry, noting that the same speaker may use multiple varieties smoothly in a single conversation.

title: CIC 7 Task 3
listening_script: When living things change their surroundings, they often change life for many other species, too. Let me give you two clear examples. First, prairie dogs—they’re small burrowing rodents that live in large colonies on North American grasslands. As they dig tunnels and rooms underground, they loosen and mix the soil. They also leave small piles of soil around the openings. After a rain, a bit of water collects there, and the ground holds moisture longer. That makes it easier for certain grasses and wildflowers to grow. Insects and small reptiles use the openings for shade or to hunt. Even if a colony moves away, the changed soil remains, so later animals and plants benefit from what the prairie dogs did earlier. That’s a simple case of “ecological inheritance.” Second, oysters—shellfish that live in shallow coastal water and attach to hard surfaces. As oysters grow, their shells build up into reefs—low, hard ridges on the seafloor. Those reefs slow the water a little, which creates calmer spots. Fine particles settle out, the water can become a bit clearer nearby, and small fish and crabs hide in the cracks between shells. Plants can also take root more easily in the quieter areas next to the reef. Even if many oysters die, the reef stays for years, attracting new oysters that add to the structure. So, in both examples—prairie dog towns on land and oyster reefs in the water—organisms don’t just adapt to an environment; they modify it and leave changes that shape future communities.
question_text: Using the examples of the prairie dog and the oyster, explain niche construction.
reading_body: Niche construction occurs when organisms actively modify their surroundings in ways that change resource availability, physical conditions, or the distribution of other species. These environmental changes can, in turn, alter the selection pressures acting on the constructors themselves and on other organisms. Niche construction differs from ordinary adaptation because it focuses on how organisms change the environment, not just how they adjust to it. The effects can be short-term—like altering soil moisture during a season—or long-lasting, when structures or chemical changes persist. Researchers sometimes call these lasting effects ecological inheritance, because later generations experience environments shaped by the activities of earlier ones.

title: CIC 8 Task 3
listening_script: Let me tell you a quick story from my department that, uh, really drove this home for me. A while back we hired a small firm to build a new event website for our program. We paid a deposit, held meetings, sent content—the whole thing. Weeks went by, the draft looked clunky, and the features we needed weren’t working. My students said, “We could switch to a simpler template and finish it ourselves.” But I kept saying, “We’ve already put so much into this.” We scheduled another round of fixes… then another. Each time I thought, “We can’t quit now—we’d waste the money we’ve already spent.” Meanwhile the event deadline was getting closer. Finally, one afternoon, a student asked me, “If we started today with the template, would it be ready by next week?” The answer was yes. If we stayed with the firm, we’d need more meetings, more delays, and probably more fees. That’s when it clicked: I was letting sunk costs—the deposit and the time already gone—drive the decision. We switched. The students launched the site in a few days, and the event went smoothly. The deposit was gone either way, but from that moment forward, the template clearly had the better future payoff.
question_text: Using points and examples from the lecture, explain the sunk cost fallacy.
reading_body: The sunk cost fallacy occurs when people let past, non-recoverable costs influence a current decision. Money, time, or effort that has already been spent cannot be regained, so rational choices should depend only on future costs and future benefits. However, individuals and organizations often keep investing in a failing plan simply because they have “come this far” or “already paid so much.” This tendency can lead to larger losses, delays, and missed opportunities. Avoiding the sunk cost fallacy requires focusing on expected outcomes from now on, even if that means abandoning a plan and accepting that earlier spending will not be recovered.

title: CIC 9 Task 3
listening_script: So, last month, our class ran a small archaeology dig at an old house site near a dry stream. Our goal was to construct a timeline of events by looking at the layers in the ground. First, in the house area, we opened a small square hole. At the bottom, we reached a hard-packed floor. Right on top of it, sat a thin ash band—evidence of a fire that happened. Above the ash was a light, dusty layer, which suggests the place sat unused for a while. At the very top, we found a stone walkway laid across the area. If you read from bottom to top, the order of events is: floor constructed, fire, area left unused, walkway constructed. So the walkway is the youngest feature, built long after the house was used and burned. We then moved to a flat spot near the stream and opened another test pit. In a light brown layer, we found a small cluster of broken pieces of a clay pot lying flat together—likely a jar that was dropped there. Directly on top of those pieces was a thin sheet of fine silt left by a later flood. The stack is clear: pot first, then flood silt on top. So the pottery is older, and the flood that buried it came after. So, in both places—by the house and by the stream—the clear stacking of layers let us build a simple timeline: lower is older, upper is younger.
question_text: Using points and examples from the lecture, explain the rule of superposition in the context of archaeology.
reading_body: At an archaeology site, dirt builds up over time in layers. If the ground has not been moved or mixed, the lower layer was put down earlier, so it is older than the layer above it. By writing down which layer sits on top of which, researchers can make a simple timeline of events—what happened first, next, and later—even without exact dates. This rule works best when the layers are still in their original order. If people or animals dig holes and mix things, the order is harder to read, so archaeologists look for places where the layers are clear and stacked in a normal way.

title: CIC 10 Task 3
listening_script: Let me illustrate this with a quick classroom study involving two groups, one item, but with one difference: ownership. The item was a campus mug, and students were randomly split. Group A were the Sellers, and each received a mug. I asked them to write the lowest price at which they’d give it up. Group B were the Buyers, and did not receive a mug. They looked at the same mug on the desk and wrote the highest price they’d pay to get one. They were all in the same room at the same time, but students answered privately so as not to influence each other. When we compared the numbers, the pattern was clear. On average, Sellers named higher amounts to part with the mug than Buyers were willing to pay to obtain it. The mug didn’t change. What changed was how people felt about it. Sellers thought of it as their mug and pictured losing it. Buyers thought about their money and what else they could buy. Those different feelings pulled the two numbers apart. So this shows that once people own an object, they tend to value keeping it more than others value getting it. That steady gap—owners asking more than non-owners will pay—is what we call the endowment effect.
question_text: Using points and examples from the lecture, explain the endowment effect.
reading_body: The endowment effect is the idea that people value an object more after they own it. Once something becomes “mine,” giving it up often feels unpleasant, so owners set a higher price to part with it. By contrast, people who do not own the same object think about other things they could buy with their money, so the amount they’re willing to pay stays lower. This difference can appear quickly, even with ordinary items like mugs or pens, and even after very short ownership. The key point is simple: ownership changes how the object feels and raises the value people place on keeping it.
